summary: For 5-6 year-olds, 'making sense of a problem' means treating a word problem as a real situation to understand before touching any number. Proficient young solvers restate what the story asks in their own words, represent it with objects or a drawing, work toward an answer, then check whether it makes sense in the story. The main teaching risk is the opposite habit — grabbing the numbers and 'doing a sum' (suspension of sense-making / compulsion to calculate). The core activity is a patient spoken 'thinking partner' routine that refuses a blurted number and builds comprehension first; concrete counters, numberless/progressively-revealed staging, a worked-example reveal, and a single reasonableness check are supporting approaches with different purposes.
misconceptions: 'I look for the special word — altogether means add, left means take away' (keyword strategy, applied before the story is even read)
'Every problem is just a sum with the numbers in it' — computes an answer even for an unanswerable or nonsensical story (suspension of sense-making / compulsion to calculate)
Restating a salient number from the story instead of the quantity actually asked for
Treating being stuck as 'I can't do it' rather than a cue to represent the story a different way

activities.title: The thinking partner who won't take a number yet
steps: Listen to a tiny within-10 spoken story from a friendly partner character, e.g. 'Three frogs were on a log and two more hopped on.'
Before giving any answer, retell the story in your own words and say what is being asked ('what are we trying to find out?').
Show the story with counters/frogs or fingers ('show me with your frogs') so the part-part-whole structure is visible.
Work out an answer for a solvable story, then answer the partner's closing question: 'Does your answer make sense in the story?'
When the partner occasionally tells a deliberately silly story ('...so what colour is the pond?' or '...so how old is the cat?'), catch that it cannot be worked out and say why.
activities.insight: A word problem is a situation to understand, not just numbers to do a sum with; sense-making and a reasonableness check come before and after calculating.

activities.title: Numberless, progressively-revealed story with a part-whole workspace
steps: See the story picture first, then the question, with the numbers revealed last.
With a workspace of draggable counters and a part-whole mat, place objects to model the situation and the relationship between the quantities.
Only after modelling, use the number pad that appears to find the answer.
Respond to a 'does this match the story?' check that compares your model to the situation, not just the final number.
activities.insight: Children reason about the relationship between quantities before a number invites them to compute, building a visual representation of the situation.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal worked example of the four moves
steps: Work through one story where each phase can be revealed: understand → represent → solve → check.
At each phase, see what a good solver asks themselves ('What is happening? What do I need to find? Does my answer make sense?').
Echo the self-questioning routine aloud after seeing it modelled.
activities.insight: The understand/represent/solve/check routine becomes visible as a sequence a solver actually follows.

activities.title: Single reasonableness check (which answer could not be right?)
steps: Given a within-10 story and a candidate answer, decide whether the answer could be right and explain why or why not.
For example: 'Maya has 6 stickers and gives some away. Could she end up with MORE than 6 stickers? How do you know?'
Explain using the situation ('fewer than 6 because she gave some away'), not by re-doing the sum.
activities.insight: Reasonableness is judged by the situation, so an answer can be ruled out before or without recomputing.

checkQuestion: Read the child a short within-10 story, e.g. 'Maya had 6 stickers. She gave 2 to her friend.' Then, before asking for any answer, ask: 'What is this story about — can you tell it back to me in your own words? What are we trying to find out? Show me how you'd work it out.' Finish with: 'How would you know if your answer makes sense?' Treat it as a discussion, not a test — you are surfacing how the child thinks about problems, not marking a number right or wrong.
checkAnswer: There is no single scored answer — listen for a child who first makes sense of the situation: retells the story in their own words, names what is being asked (how many Maya has left), represents it (moves 6 counters and takes 2 away, or draws), gives 4, and can say why 4 makes sense (she started with 6 and lost some, so it must be fewer than 6). The disposition, not the arithmetic, is the target.
